body:
> While a GLSL shader would probably be a better option, no one has implemented it yet, and I don't have any experience implementing shaders in the Godot source code. Also, nowadays, in devices where the GPU is the bottleneck, doing the conversion in the CPU might give better overall performance.

Wouldn't a shader be a *lot* less code than libyuv?

There is some precedent of shaders being used to render specific nodes, e.g. fonts with MSDF enabled or with LCD subpixel optimization enabled (which requires special alpha blending to be performed to look correct). You could ask @bruvzg to see if it would be a good option for YUV → RGB conversion. There's a shader I found [here](https://gist.github.com/jamie-pate/c30b49e10238ebcf844fee04c0b2b832) from https://github.com/kidrigger/godot-videodecoder/issues/37.

> Also, nowadays, in devices where the GPU is the bottleneck, doing the conversion in the CPU might give better overall performance.

I generally expect CPU bottlenecks to be more of a problem nowadays, especially since most games struggle to make use of multiple threads (it's not always that simple to scale to many cores). Average GPU processing power has also historically progressed faster than CPU power, especially single-core CPU power.

Also, when playing fullscreen videos where nothing else is happening, using the GPU should result in reduced power consumption (and therefore better battery life).

> > While a GLSL shader would probably be a better option, no one has implemented it yet, and I don't have any experience implementing shaders in the Godot source code. Also, nowadays, in devices where the GPU is the bottleneck, doing the conversion in the CPU might give better overall performance.
> 
> Wouldn't a shader be a _lot_ less code than libyuv?

Probably, yes. libyuv does more than pixel format conversion. The unused code could be removed but it's still more code since it has assembler for various platforms while GLSL is standard.

> There is some precedent of shaders being used to render specific nodes, e.g. fonts with MSDF enabled or with LCD subpixel optimization enabled (which requires special alpha blending to be performed to look correct). You could ask @bruvzg to see if it would be a good option for YUV → RGB conversion. There's a shader I found [here](https://gist.github.com/jamie-pate/c30b49e10238ebcf844fee04c0b2b832) from [kidrigger/godot-videodecoder#37](https://github.com/kidrigger/godot-videodecoder/issues/37).

I'll take a look at the examples you've given, that could help me get started. Thanks.

Edit: We'd still lack a faster RGBA to YUV conversion since I guess shaders couldn't help there.

After looking at the way MSDF and LCD shaders are implemented, I see that it involves mostly changes in the rendering server. If I should be changing the rendering server, I'm wondering if I shouldn't instead try to go for godotengine/godot-proposals#8049 instead. Probably more complicated for me, but if we're going to go for the best way to implement it, maybe worth considering.

The two possible options I'm evaluating:

- Implementing `CanvasItem::add_yuv4XX_texture_rect` method, passing 3 textures for the Y, Cr and Cb planes.
- Implementing a new `PlanarTexture` class, with types YUV420, YUV422 and YUV444. 

In both cases, I guess I would implement the conversion in the canvas shader, the same as MSDF and LCD.

This would be my first serious foray into the rendering server and modern graphics programming, so I would have to take some learning.

@bruvzg, can you point me in the right direction?

> Any progress on this one?

I'm waiting for someone to point me in the right direction first.
